Kenya Red Cross personnel wearing personal protective equipment simulate the evacuation of the remains of an Ebola victim in Nairobi, Kenya, on October 22, 2026 [AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 23 Oct 202623 Oct 2026
Kenya has announced its second Ebola death, as the virus outbreak spreads from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to several parts of Africa.
The Kenyan Ministry of Health said on Friday that the latest death was that of a 65-year-old woman who had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a Kenyan man who died ⁠⁠of Ebola earlier this month.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Nigeria confirms first Ebola case amid concerns about continental spreadlist 2 of 3Nigeria’s first Ebola case matches DR Congo strain, health officials saylist 3 of 3WHO warns ‘more complex’ Ebola outbreak now present in 3 African countriesend of list
The ministry added that Kenya currently has seven Ebola cases receiving treatment at two isolation facilities.
All the cases are within “one cluster, with no evidence of community spread”, it added.
Kenya’s first Ebola case was identified this month in a man who travelled from DRC to Kenya and died at ‌‌a Nairobi hospital on October 5.
Since then, Kenyan authorities have traced 135 contacts, all of whom were placed in quarantine, with nine cases confirmed, including the two patients who died.
African outbreak
The DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak in May and has since reported more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,600 deaths. The deadly disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.

An election campaign billboard featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other politicians reads in Hebrew: 'It's either the Right or Palestine' [File: Ariel Schalit/AP]By Nida IbrahimPublished On 23 Oct 202623 Oct 2026
The first Israeli elections in four years have brought with them a record number of first-time voters – most of whom are keen to make their voices count.
But while youth around the world are leaning to the left, young adults in Israel are heading in the opposite direction, according to recent polls.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3On Iran, Israel’s opposition is even more hawkish than Netanyahulist 2 of 3Ultra-Orthodox conscription debate ignites Israel’s election battlegroundlist 3 of 3In Israel election, Palestinian citizens weigh fear against disillusionmentend of list
The Israeli Central Elections Committee says more than half a million voters were added to the roll since the last elections in 2022. They are aged between 18 and 22 and polls show that 80 percent of them plan to vote in the October 27 legislative election.
Although their political activism and engagement in the public sphere are limited, a survey by the think tank, Israel Democracy Institute (IDI), found that a majority of young Jewish Israelis feel that the ballot box can influence reality and shape their country’s future.
But what does the future they hope for look like?
Around three quarters of Jewish first-time voters polled identified as “right or centre-right”, according to a recent poll for Israel’s Channel 12. That’s significantly higher than the rest of the Israeli population, which has already been shifting to the right for years.

Anna Gomez, the sole Democratic member of the United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC), called on the National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) to ramp up its response to pressure from the administration of US President Donald Trump on major news networks and broadcast television stations in advance of the midterm elections on November 3.
“I would not be doing my job if I did not say plainly that the volume of that response has not yet matched the scale of what your members are facing,” Gomez said in a four-page letter to the industry group’s CEO and President Curtis LeGeyt on Thursday.

Yemeni people inspect a damaged ambulance in front of al-Thawra General Hospital in Taiz on October 22, 2026 [Ahmad al-Basha/AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff and AFPPublished On 23 Oct 202623 Oct 2026
A mounting humanitarian disaster is gripping Yemen’s Taiz after nearly three weeks of a Houthi siege that has prevented supplies from entering the city, the United Nations has warned.
The Iran-backed Houthis have encircled Taiz since early October, cutting off the road that links it to Aden, which serves as the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Yemenis face severe shortages in Taiz amid Houthi blockadelist 2 of 4Cookies and weapons: Women in Yemen’s Taiz find ways to help the city’s defencelist 3 of 4Yemen’s government accuses Houthis of airport attacks in Aden, Mukallalist 4 of 4Fighting rages in Yemen’s Taiz as UN warns nearly 260,000 displacedend of list
Little fuel, food or other supplies have reached the city since.
“It’s 20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off,” Jens Laerke, spokesperson for the UN’s humanitarian arm, OCHA, told a news conference in Geneva on Friday. “We are seeing increasingly that the fighting makes it impossible for us to get in and impossible for people to get out.”
Most people depend on water brought in by trucks, the cost of which has tripled, Laerke said. Cooking gas is also “largely unavailable”, threatening community kitchens that provide meals to families.
Altogether, more than 800,000 people in Taiz are cut off from aid, about three-quarters of whom depend on humanitarian assistance, according to the UN World Food Programme (WFP). At least 200,000 are women and children.

Notes are seen outside Omar's office in Washington on Monday [Mariam Zuhaib/AP]By Catherine NouhanPublished On 23 Oct 202623 Oct 2026
United States President Donald Trump has called for Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar to resign from the US Congress, reviving allegations of identity fraud after a court filing identified the Minnesota politician by an additional name.
The DOJ filing, submitted on Wednesday, refers to Omar as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar” – “a/k/a” is an abbreviation for “also known as”.

The document filed by the administration does not establish that Omar committed fraud.
In response to allegations that Ilhan Omar is not her real name, the lawmaker posted on X, “So let’s make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar”.
The controversy follows a federal investigation into Omar’s immigration history and a search of her Washington, DC, home on October 12.
Omar has said she plans to move out of the home, citing safety concerns.
Here is how it all unfolded.
October 12: Federal agents search Omar’s home
Federal agents searched Omar’s Washington, DC, residence under a “judicially authorised search warrant” as part of an ongoing criminal investigation. It reportedly concerns allegations that Omar or her late father provided false information on immigration paperwork when the family fled Somalia and came to the United States in 1995, when she was a child. Mehdi Hasan debates ex-Trump adviser Steve Cortes on the economy, Trump’s immigration policies and Islamophobia.Read more
With the US midterm elections approaching, the balance of power in Congress is at stake, and the outcome could shape the legacy of President Donald Trump’s second term. As Republicans face growing voter dissatisfaction, Trump’s record has become a central battleground in the fight to control Congress.
Trump faces mounting challenges, including low approval ratings, an unpopular war in Iran, high inflation and petrol prices, economic uncertainty surrounding his tariff policies, and widespread backlash over his immigration crackdown.
How does Trump’s second term measure up against the promises he made on the campaign trail?
In this interview, Mehdi Hasan goes head-to-head with Steve Cortes, a former Trump campaign adviser, who defends the president’s second-term agenda, including his economic and immigration policies, and Islamophobic rhetoric.
Joining the discussion:
Olivia Troye – Former homeland security and counterterrorism adviser to Vice President Mike Pence
